title: Affine rigidity and Gaussian exactness in squared-distance Gromov–Wasserstein transport
shortTitle: Twelve, or under 76/7: when the Gaussian shortcut for Gromov–Wasserstein is exact
oneLine: Matching a standard Gaussian plane to a standard Gaussian line, the closed-form Gaussian Gromov–Wasserstein answer is 12, but a curved rearrangement that keeps the line exactly Gaussian provably scores below 76/7 ≈ 10.86; the paper shows the Gaussian shortcut is exact if and only if the two spectra are proportional, and is never off by more than a factor of two.
abstract: Gromov–Wasserstein (GW) transport compares two datasets or shapes that may live in different spaces by matching their internal pairwise distances. It is expensive to compute, so a closed-form answer for Gaussian data, found by Delon, Desolneux and Salmona (2022) after restricting attention to Gaussian couplings, is an attractive shortcut; those authors conjectured that the restriction loses nothing, and Peyré (October 2026) gave a first counterexample in sufficiently high dimension. For the standard squared-distance objective this candidate shows exactly when the shortcut is right: two Gaussians of positive rank admit an optimal coupling that is itself Gaussian if and only if their covariances have the same rank and proportional ordered eigenvalues. In every other case, including equal dimensions, an explicit nonlinear coupling that keeps both marginals exactly Gaussian does strictly better. The Gaussian excess is bracketed on both sides by quantities computable from the two spectra, and the Gaussian formula never overstates the optimum by more than a factor of two, a constant approached by nearly isotropic spectra in high dimension. For a standard Gaussian plane matched to a standard Gaussian line, the Gaussian answer is 12, an explicit coupling is certified below 76/7 ≈ 10.86 (about 10.47 numerically), and the true optimum lies between 8.68 and 10.85. Necessity comes from a general affine rigidity theorem: for a source whose support has interior points, an affine map is GW-optimal onto its image only if it is a similarity. The plug-in Gaussian formula on sample covariances is an inconsistent estimator for nonproportional spectra. The unrestricted optimum for nonproportional spectra is not computed. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Exactness (Theorem 5, proof): two positive-rank Gaussians admit a jointly Gaussian unrestricted optimiser of squared-distance GW if and only if their positive ranks agree and their ordered positive covariance eigenvalues are proportional; the conjecture of Delon, Desolneux and Salmona fails on every other pair, including equal dimensions. Sufficiency is due to Delon et al.

Affine rigidity (Theorem 3, proof): for a source with finite fourth moment and support with interior points in its affine hull, an affine map is GW-optimal onto its image if and only if it is a similarity or a constant.

Size of the error (Theorem 8, Corollary 9, proof): with S = ‖a‖²‖b‖² − (a·b)², S/(‖a‖‖b‖) ≤ Q_G − Q_* ≤ 8(‖a‖‖b‖ − a·b), so Q_G/2 ≤ Q_* ≤ Q_G, with the factor two approached by nearly isotropic spectra in high dimension. The upper bound is due to Delon et al.; the lower bound is new.

Plane to line (Section 7, proof with numerical refinements): the Gaussian value is 12; an explicit Gaussian-preserving coupling scores below 76/7 ≈ 10.86 (about 10.47 numerically); 8.68 ≤ Q_* ≤ 10.85, refined numerically to about 8.82 ≤ Q_* ≤ 10.03.

Plug-in inconsistency (Lemma 11, Proposition 12, proof): for nonproportional spectra the empirical GW value converges to Q_* while the plug-in Gaussian formula on sample covariances converges to Q_G ≠ Q_*.

narration: Twelve, or less than eleven? An Evidence Press briefing on comparing Gaussian data that live in different spaces. Suppose one dataset is a cloud of points spread over a plane, and another is a cloud along a line. Gromov–Wasserstein transport compares them by pairing the points up so that distances within one cloud match distances within the other as closely as possible. It is widely used, but expensive to compute. For bell-shaped, Gaussian data there is a tempting shortcut: a formula found in 2022 by Delon, Desolneux and Salmona, who searched only over Gaussian pairings and conjectured that nothing is lost by doing so. In October 2026, Gabriel Peyré showed that the shortcut can fail when a line is compared with a space of many dimensions. This paper settles exactly when the shortcut is right. It is right if, and only if, the two datasets vary in the same number of directions, and their spreads along those directions are in the same proportions. In every other case, even for two datasets of the same dimension, a curved rearrangement that keeps both clouds exactly Gaussian does strictly better. Take a standard Gaussian plane and a standard Gaussian line. The shortcut scores twelve, where lower is better. The paper builds a curved pairing that provably scores below seventy-six sevenths, about ten point eight six, and it proves that the true best score lies between eight point six eight and ten point eight five. In general, the error is bracketed from both sides and is never more than a factor of two. And when the proportions differ, plugging sample covariances into the formula gives an estimate that converges to the wrong value. The theorems have written proofs and computer checks, including deliberately planted errors that the checks catch. The true optimum, when the proportions differ, is still unknown. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on the first of November twenty twenty-six, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: Use the closed-form Gaussian GW value as the true squared-distance GW value only when the two covariance spectra have equal positive rank and are proportional; otherwise report the certified bracket Q_G − 8(‖a‖‖b‖ − a·b) ≤ Q_* ≤ Q_G − S/(‖a‖‖b‖), which always lies within a factor of two.
decisionObject.scope: Squared-distance GW with squared loss between Gaussian marginals. Non-Gaussian data, entropic, inner-product and ordinary-distance GW are not covered.
